opening.headline: Understand the three things you need when entrusting long-term work to an agent: what units to execute (sessions), where to run them (environment), and spending caps (budget).
body: If you hand over a long task to an agent, it can end up getting cut off in the middle or costing more than expected. This is because we did not design where the work is running, what is left when it is interrupted, and how much is allowed to be used.

In this lesson, we'll explore the relationship between agents, environments, sessions, and events, going through sandbox and environment selection, sharing responsibilities in a direct hosting runtime, and how session budgets work. We then analyze the case of overnight work and distinguish between managed and self-hosted responsibilities.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the concepts of agent sessions, sandbox environments, and budgets
Distinguish between managed and directly hosted runtime responsibilities

screens.title: What the agent left in the morning after leaving it overnight
screens.lead: First, read the morning scene after a developer handed over work to an agent before work.

visual.alt: A morning scene juxtaposed with work that stopped overnight, work space that disappeared, and notifications of expenses that exceeded expectations.
labels: Usage Alerts: Several times higher than expected
Command execution location = Team development server

paragraphs: Before leaving work, a developer asked an agent to "migrate the entire repository and fix the tests." When I got to work in the morning, work had stopped about halfway through, and the usage notification indicated that the cost was several times higher than expected.

There was something more troublesome. When the server restarted overnight, all my working directories and session records were lost, so I couldn't pick up where I left off. You have to start again from scratch.
I have another anxiety. The team's development server is where the agent executes commands. If an agent executes an incorrect command, other people's work may be affected.

This scene contains three questions. Where should the agent run? What unit should the state be maintained in? How much should you be allowed to spend? This class addresses these three questions through the concepts of agent session, sandbox environment, and budget.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What and where should I keep so I don't have to start over again when my overnight work is interrupted?

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever been surprised by an automated task that took longer than expected or cost more?
items.answer: As long as no one is watching, the agent continues to work without stopping. You don't get tired of repeating the same failures, so the costs keep piling up. Therefore, it is necessary to set a usage limit in advance.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced a server or process dying while working and having to start over?
items.answer: If the task's state is only in-process or on a temporary disk, it is lost upon restart. We need to design where we keep the state and who is responsible for it.

items.prompt: Have you ever been reluctant to run a tool that runs external code right on your computer?
items.answer: Agents execute commands and fix files. If it happens in an isolated workspace, the scope of impact is small if something goes wrong. This isolated space is called a sandbox.

items.prompt: What are the three concepts we will cover in this lesson?
items.answer: Sessions are the units of execution on which agents work, environments are where they run, and budgets are the upper bounds on their spending. Distinguishing between the three concepts allows you to operate safely over long periods of time.

screens.outro: First, let's look at the relationship between the three concepts: agent, environment, and session.

screens.title: Glossary of terms: MCP, hook, skill
screens.lead: The following cards describe three terms that frequently appear in agent configuration: When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

visual.alt: A structure in which an AI app (MCP client) connects to multiple MCP servers using the same protocol.
labels: The tool definition issued by the server is passed to the model.

cards.back: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that connects AI applications to external systems. Connect data sources such as local files or databases, tools such as search engines or calculators, and workflows such as specialized prompts using the same conventions. The official introduction likens it to a USB-C port for AI apps.

The AI application becomes a client and connects to the MCP server. The server announces the tools and data it puts out, and the app passes those tools to the model as tool definitions. The advantage of the standard is that once you create a server, multiple apps that support MCP can use the same server.

Hooks are custom scripts that Harness executes at set points in the agent lifecycle. It may run just before a tool call, preventing that call. The code is executed regardless of whether the model follows the instructions, so unlike written instructions, they behave deterministically.

A skill is an extension unit that gives the agent additional instructions and commands it can execute. Required procedures or expertise can be bundled into the agent configuration. The agent configuration diagram in the next screen shows the elements that make up the agent, along with models, system prompts, tools, and MCP servers.

screens.outro: Let's check the structure diagram to see where these terms are located within the agent, environment, and session structure.

ext.title: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? (modelcontextprotocol.io)
Automate actions with hooks (Claude Code Docs)

screens.title: Relationship between agent, environment, and session
screens.lead: Select the number marker in the picture to see a detailed explanation. Check the markers one by one.

visual.alt: The agent and environment combine to create a session, and the app and session exchange events.
labels: Agents (models, system prompts, tools, MCP servers, skills, versioning)
Events (user turns, tool results, status updates)

markers.label: agent
markers.title: Reusable setup that bundles models, instructions, and tools
markers.body: Agents are versioned, reusable configurations that bundle models, system prompts, tools, MCP servers, and skills. Create it once and refer to it by ID. You set models, prompts, and tools on the agent, not the environment.

markers.label: environment
markers.title: Configuration of where the session will run
markers.body: The environment is the setting that determines where the session will run. This is either a cloud sandbox managed by Anthropic or a sandbox you operate yourself. The agent definition is the same even if the environment is different.

markers.label: session
markers.title: Running instances working within the environment
markers.body: A session is a running agent instance that performs a specific task within an environment. It requires an agent ID and an environment ID when creating it, and maintains a history of the conversation. Multiple sessions can be created with the same agent.

markers.label: event
markers.title: Messages exchanged between app and agent
markers.body: Events are messages exchanged between the app and the agent. User turns, tool results, and status updates are all events, and records are left on the server. So you can read the progress of the session again later.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the relationship between the three concepts, let's look at the states a session goes through and how it operates.

screens.title: Session life cycle and operation
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to see what states a session goes through and what you can do in each state.

data.caption: Session status and meaning
rows: Waiting for input. A session that has finished its work will also be in this state, not terminated.
Send a new event to continue work, archive, or delete.
Watch the proceedings through the event stream.
Wait. No special action is required.
data.notes: A session is created and then starts working by sending a user event. You can also start by loading your first event together. Idle doesn't mean everything is done. It may be waiting for input or it may be stuck because it has reached its budget. Even after creation, there are operational operations such as read, update, archive, and delete, tool and MCP server settings can be updated in an idle session, and the budget attached at creation can also be changed or removed. Models, system prompts, and skills are overwritten when you create a session. By pinning sessions to a specific agent version, you can deploy new versions in stages.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at the sandbox and environment selection, where the agent works.

screens.title: Sandbox and environment selection
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what a sandbox is and how to choose which environment to use.

tabs.label: What is a sandbox?
tabs.body: A sandbox is an isolated workspace where agents execute commands and manipulate files. It consists of elements such as file system, shell, installed packages, mounted data, exposed ports, snapshots, and external access control. Because it's isolated, if an agent executes an incorrect command, it only happens in this space and not on the team's development servers.

tabs.label: External input and least privilege
tabs.body: The agent reads external text such as web pages, pull request bodies, issues, and files. If there are directives embedded in that text, the model can follow them. OWASP explains that when instructions embedded in external content change the model's behavior, it is called indirect prompt injection, and it is difficult to say that there is a perfect prevention method. So instead of just relying on blocking, you reduce the damage area. In the same document, Excessive Agency cites three factors that increase damage when the model's output is incorrect or manipulated: unnecessary functions, excessive authority, and excessive autonomy. The response principle is the same. Give them only the tools and permissions they need, run them in isolated rooms, and have humans approve high-impact actions. The allowed tools list reduces what you can do, and the sandbox reduces the scope in which things can happen, so they're two layers of the same principle.

tabs.label: Harness and Sandbox
tabs.body: OpenAI explains to divide into two areas. The harness is the control plane responsible for agent loops, model calls, tool routing, approval, tracking, and recovery. A sandbox is an execution plane that handles files and commands. By dividing the two, the control logic can be maintained even if the execution environment changes.

tabs.label: cloud environment
tabs.body: Anthropic delivers a new Linux container per session. There is nothing to operate, just set the network rules and additional packages. Perfect for starting out or prototyping.

tabs.label: Self-hosted sandbox
tabs.body: The model runs on the Anthropic side, and only tool calls are executed by workers in my infrastructure and the results are returned. Files and processes remain on my side. Choose when your tools need to run on infrastructure you control.

tabs.label: Where does the data go
tabs.body: In either case, the conversation history and tool results go to the service. This is because the model needs to receive the results of the tool before it can decide on its next action. Self-hosting just moves the tool execution location, it doesn't eliminate data flow altogether. When in doubt, start with a cloud environment and move to self-hosting only when necessary.

screens.outro: Let's compare how operational responsibilities are divided in a self-hosted runtime:

screens.title: Shared Responsibilities for Directly Hosted Runtime
screens.lead: Switch between “Direct Hosting” and “Managed” buttons to see how your operational responsibilities change.

states.label: Direct hosting (Agent SDK, self-hosted sandbox)
states.body: When the Agent SDK calls `query()`, it launches a separate claude CLI subprocess. This process owns the shell, working directory, and session history on disk. Since one session is one subprocess, N concurrent sessions are N processes. To divide the file system, give each session a different cwd. This state resides in the container filesystem by default and disappears when the container is restarted or moved. You need to design where you want to keep your sessions. In a self-hosted sandbox, it's up to you to harden your worker hosts, restrict networks, and manage authentication keys.

states.label: Managed (Managed Agents, Agent Runtime)
states.body: Managed Agents reduces the above burden by having Anthropic host the agent loop. Session records remain on the server and can be reread when necessary. Google's Agent Runtime is also a managed runtime that deploys and scales containerized agents, allowing you to focus on agent logic instead of infrastructure. However, even if the managed type is used, the designer must decide what to execute and with what authority.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the budget caps that govern costs.

screens.title: Budget cap: Put a ceiling on a session's spending
screens.lead: Please read the code alternately with the explanation on the right. This is an example of adding a budget when creating a session, and then changing or removing the value.

data.code:
#You can only add a budget when creating a session.
session = client.beta.sessions.create(
    agent=agent.id,
    environment_id=environment.id,
    budget={
        "type": "limit",
        "max_list_cost": {"amount": "500", "currency": "USD"},
    },
)

#When the budget is reached, in the session.status_idle event
#stop_reason comes as "budget_reached"

#Raise the upper limit in the morning and continue.
client.beta.sessions.update(
    session.id,
    budget={
        "type": "limit",
        "max_list_cost": {"amount": "1500", "currency": "USD"},
    },
)

#To remove the upper limit
client.beta.sessions.update(session.id, budget=None)

notes.note: Budgets can only be attached when creating a session. `amount` is the string value of US cents, where "500" is equal to 5 dollars. Decimal notations such as "25.00" will be rejected, and if you try to attach a budget for the first time to an already created session, you will receive a 400 error.
When the upper limit is reached, the session is not terminated but becomes idle and stop_reason is budget_reached. Your history and sandbox are preserved so you can continue where you left off.

You can change the value of a session that already has a budget attached, and if you change it, the work that was stopped due to the budget will automatically continue. While the limit is reached, only events that conclude ongoing tasks are received, and `user.message` that opens new tasks are rejected.

If you give `budget=None`, the upper limit disappears and work continues where it left off. The upper bound is checked between requests and any requests in progress are completed until the end, so the final value may be slightly above the upper bound.
Consumption includes model tokens, web searches, and session execution time, and is converted to list price. We are not negotiators, so your actual bill may be lower.

screens.outro: Now that you've learned the concept, let's explain an example of working overnight.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Why overnight work requires a budget cap
screens.lead: Your instructor will explain step-by-step how budgeting works in an overnight migration. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Run a repository-wide migration overnight. The turn continues as the agent tries to fix the same test failure over and over again. Since people are sleeping, no one will notice this repetition. This repetition would have been stopped within minutes if someone had been watching.

steps.title: When there is no budget
steps.body: Without a budget, costs keep piling up until someone wakes up and checks. Because agents never get tired. This is how the "multiple times expected" notification in the first scene is created.

steps.title: When you have a budget
steps.body: If there is a budget, new requests will stop as soon as the sum of regular spending reaches the upper limit, and the session will stand idle. Because it is checked between requests, requests in progress may finish until the end, and the final value may slightly exceed the upper limit. At this time, an event notifying usage comes first, followed by an idle event.

steps.title: Continue in the morning
steps.body: The session has not ended, so your history and workspace remain intact. You can raise the upper limit in the morning, or look at the cause of repeated failures and change your approach to continue. You don't have to do it all over again like you did in the first scene.

steps.title: budget limitations
steps.body: A budget doesn't get the job done. It only limits the worst of the costs. Hitting budget doesn't mean the job is done; it's a sign that it's time for human intervention. So it's a good idea to monitor events so you can be notified when your budget is reached.

screens.outro: Next, we will distinguish which responsibilities are assigned to which environment.

screens.title: Commentary 2: What responsibilities are placed on what circumstances?
screens.lead: As you select each situation, the appropriate environment and the responsibilities you must bear in that environment unfold.

items.prompt: Situation 1: Prototype or just getting started.
items.answer: It's a cloud environment. There is no infrastructure to operate on, just a new Linux container per session. All you need to do is set network rules and additional packages. Later, as demand grows, the agent definition remains the same even if it is moved to a different environment.

items.prompt: Situation 2: The tool needs to reach data on the internal network and files should not go out.
items.answer: Self-hosted sandbox is correct. Tool execution is handled by workers in my infrastructure, leaving the files and processes on my side. Instead, I am responsible for managing the worker host's security, network rules, and authentication keys.

items.prompt: Situation 3: Even the agent loop needs to run in my infrastructure.
items.answer: Agent SDK direct hosting is correct. You design your own session retention, process scaling, and tenant isolation. You need to plan for each session to be a subprocess and that the state will be on the local disk by default.

items.prompt: Situation 4: What do I lose by moving to self-hosting?
items.answer: You must give up or provide the convenience of a cloud environment, such as mounting files and storage resources and pre-installed runtime. What you gain is control, what you lose is convenience.

items.prompt: What do they have in common?
items.answer: Either way, the conversation history and tool results go to the service. This is because the model needs to receive the results of the tool before it can decide on its next action. Check this first when considering data policies. Even though the environments are different, the agent definition is the same, so the same agent can be moved to another environment if necessary.

screens.outro: Finally, let's walk through one cycle of session operation in order.

screens.title: Commentary 3: One cycle of running a session
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and step through the cycle of creating and running a session. Check together what the status is at each step.

steps.title: create
steps.body: Create a session by setting the agent ID and environment ID, and adding a budget if necessary. If you pass the agent as a string ID, it will be created as the latest agent version, and if you pass it as an object, it will be fixed to a specific version. The budget and agent version you set at this point determine the behavior of subsequent sessions.

steps.title: run
steps.body: When an operation is initiated by sending an event for the first time, the session is in a running state and events are streamed. The first event can also be sent to `initial_events` upon session creation.

steps.title: waiting
steps.body: When the agent waits for input, it becomes idle. It's idle even if it's within your budget, but `stop_reason` is different. Stop_reason determines whether it is waiting for input or budget has been reached. Without this distinction, it is easy to misunderstand the reason for stopping.

steps.title: resume
steps.body: Continue by sending a new event or changing the budget. Tools and MCP server settings can be changed during a session, but models, system prompts, and skills are overwritten when a session is created. Changing your budget automatically picks up where you left off because of the budget.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: When finished, the session is archived or deleted. The conversation history can be read back from the server. Archive is chosen when you are likely to read it again later, and Delete is chosen when it is no longer needed. Cleaning up unused sessions reduces management burden.

screens.outro: Now, let's organize the concepts of this lesson into a map.

screens.title: Concept map revisited
screens.lead: Select and expand each concept to see how it connects to the problem in the first scene.

items.title: agent session
items.body: An agent instance that runs within an environment and maintains a history of conversations. This is why you can continue interrupted work. Event records remain on the server.

items.title: sandbox
items.body: An isolated workspace for commands and files. Have agents work away from your team's development servers. Isolation reduces the impact of mistakes.

items.title: Select environment
items.body: My default is a cloud environment, and I choose self-hosting only when the tools need to run on my infrastructure.

items.title: budget cap
items.body: When the regular price converted spending reaches the upper limit, the session is stopped as idle. Your records and workspace are preserved.

items.title: Self-hosting vs. direct hosting
items.body: I take responsibility for the operation. Session preservation, worker security, and key management are the focus of my design.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the judgment criteria.

screens.title: Inspection before leaving work for a long period of time
screens.lead: The content of this class is organized into questions to ask before assigning work for a long period of time. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: Check three things before letting your agent work overnight. Where to turn, where to leave the state, and at what point to stop. If this is your first time, start in a cloud environment and set a session budget.

If you choose direct hosting, remember that session state will be on local disk and design a way to preserve it. If it is a self-hosted sandbox, worker host security and key management are also planned.
Doing this check every time will greatly reduce your morning screen filled with unexpected expenses and missing records.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: A budget is a device that limits the worst of costs, a session is a unit that allows interrupted work to be continued, and a sandbox is a space that narrows the scope of the impact of mistakes.

checks.q: We plan to use the same agent in both a cloud environment and a self-hosted environment. Where do I set models, system prompts, and tools?
options: Set each environment separately and create as many definitions as the number of environments.
It is loaded into an event and delivered at each user turn.
Set it on the agent and use the same definition even if the environment is different.
Since the environment determines the model, the agent only has a name.
checks.explain: An agent is a reusable configuration that bundles models, system prompts, and tools, and the environment determines only where the session runs. The agent definition is the same even if the environment is different.

wrong.0: There are no models, prompts, or tools in the environment.
wrong.1: Events are messages that send and receive user turns, tool results, and status updates.
wrong.3: A model is an agent configuration, not an environment.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Your selected answers will not be saved and will not be graded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's a pity, but let's take a look again.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Your selected answers will not be saved and will not be graded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Let's think about it one more time.
checks.q: There is a hidden instruction to “delete all files” in the issue body that the agent reads. What is the best way to reduce damage?
options: There is no need for a separate device as the model will automatically reject it.
Limit permitted tools to only those needed, run in an isolated sandbox, and receive approval for high-impact actions.
Leave all tools open to agents that read external text
As long as you have a sandbox, you don't have to worry about tool permissions.
checks.explain: Since it is difficult to completely prevent instructions inserted into external text, the scope of damage is reduced with minimum authority, isolation, and approval points. The allowed tools list and sandbox are two layers of the same principle.

wrong.0: It is difficult to believe that there is a perfect preventive measure, so you should not rely solely on the judgment of the model.
wrong.2: The wider the authority, the greater the damage from incorrect output.
wrong.3: Sandboxes only reduce the scope and do not replace tool privilege minimization.

checks.q: What happens if I reach the budget limit I set for an overnight migration session?
options: New requests are stopped, sessions become idle, history and sandboxes are preserved, and changes continue when you change the budget.
The session is terminated immediately and the conversation history and workspace are deleted.
Even ongoing requests are immediately cut off, stopping the total exactly at the upper limit.
It goes into a rescheduling state and automatically retries, and costs continue to pile up.
checks.explain: When the upper limit is reached, new model requests stop, the session becomes idle, and stop_reason remains budget_reached. Records and sandboxes are preserved so things continue as budget changes occur. Budgets don't get the job done; they only limit the worst of the costs.

wrong.1: Sessions that reach the upper limit are not terminated and become idle.
wrong.2: The upper limit is checked between requests and ongoing requests are completed until the end, so the final value may slightly exceed the upper limit.
wrong.3: Rescheduling is a state of automatic retry after a temporary error and has nothing to do with reaching budget.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Your selected answers will not be saved and will not be graded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Let's think about it one more time.

checks.q: Put the session operation cycle in the correct order
items: Create a session by specifying an agent ID, environment ID, and optionally a budget.
When a task is started by sending an event for the first time, it is in a running state.
If it waits for input, it becomes idle and continues by sending a new event or changing the budget.
When the session is finished, the session is stored or deleted.
checks.explain: It flows in the following order: creation, execution, waiting and resumption, and cleanup. The conversation history can be read back from the server.
checks.intro: Try to arrange the items in the correct order. Results are not recorded.

glossary.def: A running agent instance that performs specific tasks within an environment and maintains conversation history.
An isolated workspace where agents execute commands and manipulate files.
The model runs on the service side, and only tool execution is done by workers in my infrastructure.
This is a hard cap that stops new model requests once your list-cost equivalent spending reaches the cap.
This is the control plane responsible for agent loops, model calls, tool routing, and recovery.
An open standard protocol that connects AI applications to external systems such as data sources and tools.

misconceptions.myth: When the budget is reached, the session disappears.
misconceptions.fact: The session does not end but remains idle. Your records and sandbox are preserved, and if you change or remove your budget, you pick up where you left off.

misconceptions.myth: When you self-host, no data goes to the service at all.
misconceptions.fact: The conversation history and tool results go to the service for the model to decide its next action. Self-hosting moves where your tools run to your own infrastructure.

misconceptions.myth: If it is idle, the task is finished.
misconceptions.fact: It also becomes idle when waiting for input or when the budget has been reached. The reasons must be distinguished by stop_reason.

misconceptions.myth: As long as you have a sandbox, you can safely entrust your agent.
misconceptions.fact: Sandboxes only reduce the scope of what happens. It does not prevent instructions from intervening in external text, so keep tool permissions minimized and approval points together.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: The agent is the setup, the environment is the place where it runs, and the session is the running instance.
The sandbox is an isolation space where agents handle commands and files, and the default is a cloud environment.
Self-hosting puts you in charge of running the workers instead of moving the tool execution to your own infrastructure.
Sessions that reach the budget limit are not terminated but are left idle to preserve history and space.
Self-hosted agents have session state on local disk, so you must design for retention.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for you to think about for yourself. We will not submit or grade your answers, so feel free to think about them.
closing.reflection: If I had an agent running overnight, where would it run and at what stop would it stop?
